params.question: A researcher formulates the question: 'What is the prevalence of anaemia among pregnant women attending antenatal clinics in Andhra Pradesh in 2024?' According to the relationship between research question type and study design, which design is most appropriate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An RCT tests the efficacy of an intervention. This question asks about prevalence, not about whether an intervention works.
Case-control designs investigate causation by comparing exposures between those with and without the outcome. A prevalence question does not require this retrospective approach.
Correct. A prevalence question measures how common a condition is at a single point in time, which is exactly what a cross-sectional design captures.
Cohort studies follow subjects over time to examine causation or incidence. A prevalence question needs a single time-point measurement, not longitudinal follow-up.

overallFeedback.feedback: A prevalence question measures how common a condition is at one point in time — this calls for a cross-sectional study. Remember the mapping: prevalence → cross-sectional, causation → cohort/case-control, intervention efficacy → RCT.

Exactly right. Prevalence questions lead to cross-sectional studies, causation questions to cohort or case-control studies, and intervention efficacy questions to RCTs. The research question type is the compass for study design.

interactions.label: In a study measuring haemoglobin levels in 400 pregnant women, the researchers r

params.question: In a study measuring haemoglobin levels in 400 pregnant women, the researchers report a mean Hb of 10.2 g/dL. Which statistic tells them how precisely this sample mean estimates the true population mean?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Standard deviation describes how spread out the individual data points are around the sample mean. It characterises your sample's variability, not the precision of your estimate of the population mean.
Correct. Standard error equals SD divided by the square root of n. It quantifies how precisely the sample mean estimates the true population mean, and it shrinks as the sample size grows.

CV expresses standard deviation as a percentage of the mean, useful for comparing variability across different measurement scales. It does not address the precision of the mean as a population estimate.
IQR describes the spread of the middle 50% of observations. Like SD, it is a measure of dispersion within the sample, not a measure of how precisely the sample mean estimates the population mean.

overallFeedback.feedback: Standard deviation describes your sample's spread; standard error tells you how precisely your sample mean estimates the true population mean. SE = SD/√n, so it shrinks as the sample grows. This is one of the most commonly confused distinctions in biostatistics.

Well done. Standard error (SE = SD/√n) is the key statistic for gauging how close a sample mean is to the true population mean, and it decreases with larger sample sizes — reflecting greater precision.

interactions.label: A researcher wants to compare mean systolic blood pressure across three independ

params.question: A researcher wants to compare mean systolic blood pressure across three independent groups of patients classified as normotensive, pre-hypertensive, and hypertensive. The blood pressure values are normally distributed. Using the four-step test selection framework, which test is most appropriate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The t-test compares means between exactly two groups. With three groups, you need a test designed for simultaneous multiple-group comparison to control the false-positive rate.
Chi-square tests the association between two categorical variables. Blood pressure here is a continuous, normally distributed outcome — not a categorical one.
Mann-Whitney U is the non-parametric alternative to the independent t-test, used when data are not normally distributed and only two groups are compared. Neither condition applies here.
Correct. Walking through the framework: (1) continuous outcome, (2) three groups, (3) independent subjects, (4) normally distributed — all four steps point to one-way ANOVA.

overallFeedback.feedback: Apply the framework in order: (1) continuous outcome, (2) three groups, (3) independent, (4) normally distributed. This combination points to one-way ANOVA. A t-test handles only two groups; chi-square is for categorical data; Mann-Whitney is non-parametric and for two groups.

Exactly. The four-step framework — continuous outcome, three independent groups, normal distribution — leads directly to one-way ANOVA. Remember that ANOVA tells you groups differ overall; post-hoc tests like Tukey's or Bonferroni then identify which specific pairs differ.

params.question: A large study of 100,000 participants finds that a nutritional supplement raises mean haemoglobin by 0.05 g/dL, with p < 0.001. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

answers.text: The supplement is both statistically and clinically effective since p < 0.001

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A small p-value only means the observed difference is unlikely to be due to chance. It says nothing about whether the effect size is large enough to matter in clinical practice.

answers.text: The result is statistically significant but the effect size is too small to be clinically meaningful

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Although p < 0.001 confirms the difference is unlikely due to chance, 0.05 g/dL is smaller than most lab equipment can measure precisely and has no practical clinical importance.

answers.text: The p-value proves there is a real biological effect on haemoglobin synthesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A p-value is the probability of seeing data this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. It does not prove any hypothesis is true, nor does it describe the biological mechanism.

answers.text: The result should be rejected because 0.05 g/dL is within measurement error

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While the effect is trivially small, the result is still statistically significant. The correct response is not to reject it outright, but to recognise that statistical significance alone does not establish clinical importance.

overallFeedback.feedback: With 100,000 participants, even a tiny difference can achieve statistical significance. But 0.05 g/dL has no clinical meaning. Always separate statistical significance (is the difference real?) from clinical significance (does it matter for patient care?).

Well done. Always ask two separate questions: is the difference statistically significant, and is the effect size clinically meaningful? Large sample sizes can make trivially small differences reach statistical significance.

params.question: In the tribal block nutritional survey, the mean BMI-for-age z-score (−1.8) is lower than the median (−1.6), indicating that the distribution is positively skewed.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: When the mean is lower than the median, the distribution is negatively (left) skewed, not positively. The tail of extremely low BMI-for-age values pulls the mean below the median. Remember: the mean follows the tail — if the tail extends left, the mean shifts left of the median.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. When the mean is pulled below the median, the distribution is negatively (left) skewed. A tail of extremely low BMI-for-age values drags the mean downward. In a positive skew, the mean would be pulled above the median.
